# Scaled content abuse

*Concept*

The spam policy against producing many pages mainly to manipulate rankings, whether by AI, people or both.

**Glossary** (*Scaled content abuse*): A Google spam policy against generating many pages mainly to manipulate rankings with little value to users, however they are made, including automated translation of scraped content.

Narrative: the topic [Spam policies and manual actions](../topics/spam-policies.md) tells the story; this card lists what links to it.

10 claims mention it: 2 from Google's documentation, 4 shown or said at the event (1 not in Google docs, 1 confirmed by Google docs, 2 consistent with Google docs), 4 the author's analysis. A card is a map: cite the claim ids, with the citation given after each claim.

## Google's documentation

Documented in: [Spam policies for Google web search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies).

- [`D1-C129`](../sessions/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) Docs: Google's guide says creating separate content for every variation of how people might search, including fan-out queries, primarily to manipulate rankings or AI responses violates its scaled content abuse policy. It adds that its AI systems can understand a page's relevance even without an exact match to the query. `[D1-C129, docs, Google Search Central, https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide]`
- [`D2-C611`](../sessions/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) Docs: Google's spam policies define scaled content abuse as generating many pages mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value to users, no matter how they are created, and list automated translating of scraped content among the examples. `[D2-C611, docs, Google Search Central, https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies]`

## Shown or said at the event

Not in Google's documentation first: present those as said at Search Central Live, never as documented policy.

- [`D3-C284`](../sessions/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) Stage, Day 3, not in Google docs: Reviewing the spam slide, the speaker said link spam would probably be replaced with scaled content abuse as the spam type worth talking about today. `[D3-C284, stage, Google, Day 3]`
- [`D3-C207`](../sessions/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) Stage, Day 3, confirmed by Google docs: Google's quality talk listed recent updates to Google's spam policies: back button hijacking, scaled content abuse and manipulating AI responses. `[D3-C207, stage, Google, Day 3]`
- [`D3-C694`](../sessions/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) Stage, Day 3, consistent with Google docs: Scaled content abuse is becoming a problem again: in the early 2000s pages were churned out with Perl or PHP scripts, and now the same is done with LLMs. `[D3-C694, stage, Gary Illyes, Day 3]`
- [`D3-C695`](../sessions/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) Stage, Day 3, consistent with Google docs: The cheaper tokens become, the more AI slop is created, and Google counts AI slop as scaled content abuse. `[D3-C695, stage, Gary Illyes, Day 3]`

## The author's analysis

- [`D1-C048`](../sessions/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) Analysis: The answer is not a claim that Google detects AI text. It says ranking favours text that reads as natural to people. The risk with AI content is scale without value, which falls under Google's scaled content abuse policy, not the tool itself. `[D1-C048, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D2-C612`](../sessions/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) Analysis: Treat machine translation as a first draft: have a native speaker review it and adapt dates, calendars and units before publishing, because unreviewed bulk translation that adds little value can also fall under Google's scaled content abuse policy. `[D2-C612, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D2-C692`](../sessions/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) Analysis: The lower selection bar in under-served languages is an opening for content written for that market, not for machine translation at scale: index selection also applies spam signals, and Google's spam policies count generating many pages from scraped content through automated transformations such as translating, with little value for users, as scaled content abuse. `[D2-C692, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D3-C300`](../sessions/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) Analysis: Weight spam audits toward scaled content abuse: a Googler said that type would replace link spam on the slide, so review mass-produced pages, including AI-generated ones, before older link-building patterns. `[D3-C300, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`

## For developers

- `DEV-AIF-03` **SHOULD** · Documented: Structure content for readers instead of splitting it into small chunks for AI (1 of its claims mentions it; its own text names it)
- `DEV-INT-10` **SHOULD** · Documented: Publish machine-translated language versions only after human review and localisation (3 of its claims mention it; its own text names it)
- `DEV-SPM-02` **AVOID** · Documented: Do not generate large sets of low-value pages from templates, feeds or LLM output (5 of its claims mention it; its own text names it)
